Item Week Grading File

Featured artist (verified)

Vija Celmins (Latvian-born American artist, born 1938). Renowned for meticulous, photo-based renderings of vast natural fields, including night skies and galaxies, as well as ocean surfaces and desert floors. Her star-field works show how careful value and contrast can turn flat marks on a flat surface into the illusion of deep space. Her work is held by major collections including the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), the Whitney Museum of American Art, and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA).

Verified anchor work for this lesson: Untitled (Galaxy), from the portfolio Untitled, 1975, lithograph, 12 1/4 × 16 1/4 in. Collection of SFMOMA (acquired 1976 by purchase). Confirmed live at https://www.sfmoma.org/artwork/76.132.4/ (2026-07-14).

COPYRIGHT NOTE

Vija Celmins is a living artist (b. 1938) and her work is not in the public domain. Per the course-wide copyright rule, this work is not embedded anywhere in the module. The instructional page (01_Instructional-Page.html) instead carries a clean link-out box: title, date, medium, and holding museum, with a direct link to SFMOMA's own collection page for this print. Do not substitute an embedded image file for this artist at any point in this module.

Cross-curricular science (verified, kept simple)

  • A galaxy is a huge system of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity. Our Sun belongs to one called the Milky Way.
  • A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space. Some nebulae are regions where new stars can form.

Keep the science factual and simple; this is an art course connecting to science, not a science lesson.

Codes are stable; descriptions are paraphrased — verify exact wording at cpalms.org before any formal report. Cycle-relevant benchmarks:

Discussion board (.03)

Template: 2. Element & Principle Evidence. Twist (lead question): How do artists use contrast (bright stars, dark space) and movement (swirls, trails) to make space feel deep and alive? Artworks: Celmins, Untitled (Galaxy) (link-out only, SFMOMA) and the Whirlpool Galaxy image on the instructional page.

Criterion Points
Original post answers the full prompt with specific visual evidence 4
Uses at least 2 art vocabulary words correctly 2
2 replies that are respectful, specific, and add a new idea 4

Canvas setup tip: Under discussion options, turn on "Users must post before seeing replies."

Standards (from the author's doc): VA.68.C.1.1 (discuss structural elements and organizational principles); VA.68.H.1.1 (identify works as reflections of culture, time, and place). Verify current benchmark language at cpalms.org.

VR (.02)

Students choose a Location (an indoor space, a studio, or an outdoor scene), bring the deep-space images from the instructional page into it, and hunt for movement, contrast, color, and value. They answer three short questions (live with classmates or on their own), then draw a galaxy or build a small star-field. The Celmins print is link-out only. Students who cannot use VR do the same three parts with the images on screen or on paper, drawing on paper or arranging objects at a desk. Evidence is the same either way: a screenshot or photo plus the typed answers. The page opens with the line: "If you can complete this assignment in VR, please do so. If not, it still needs to be completed outside VR."

Quiz answer key

Full key is inside 06_Module-11.05_Short-Quiz.md (8 questions, 1.25 pts each, 10 pts total). At a glance: 1-C, 2-A, 3-D, 4-B, 5-C, 6-A, 7-True, 8-matching. Correct-answer positions are intentionally varied. Question 6 is the cross-curricular science item (what a galaxy is). Canvas stores the key in the quiz; do not expose it to students.

Materials (home-accessible)

One or two sheets of paper for the painting (heavier paper or cardstock holds wet paint better, but is not required), plus one extra sheet of paper for the brick-wall overlay, pencil, scissors, and glue or glue stick. Any paint the student has at home: watercolor, tempera, or acrylic, or even watered-down paint. A brush, plus an old toothbrush for splatter (a fingertip flick works too). A cup of water and a paper towel. All standard household supplies; nothing to purchase.

Pacing

  • Week 1: instructional page, then Module 11.01 Sketch (Stars and Swirls), Module 11.02 VR, and Module 11.03 Discussion Board. The sketch is the practice rung for the painting.
  • Week 2: Module 11.04 Studio Project & Reflection (paint the galaxy, add the broken-brick-wall overlay, submit with the artist statement), then Module 11.05 Short Quiz.

Ladder rung

Sketch = study/practice rung (try each galaxy technique by hand in isolation: a wet-on-wet blend, a swirl that creates movement, a splatter of stars). Painting = variation rung (combine the studied techniques into the student's own galaxy composition, then frame it with the broken-wall device). No rung is skipped: students practice the techniques (Week 1) before composing the full work (Week 2).

Deployment notes

  • The instructional page is the only interactive item. It deploys to the optimaondemand/mj-visual-art-3 Pages repo as module-11-instructional.html; embed the published URL in Canvas.
  • Sketch, VR, discussion board, and studio pages paste into the Canvas RCE as-is (inline-styled, no scripts).
  • The quiz is Canvas-native (Canvas Quiz).

Teacher Cycle Plan — Module 12: Post-Impressionism (Van Gogh Pop-Up Chairs)

Featured masterwork (verified)

Vincent van Gogh (Dutch, 1853–1890), a leading Post-Impressionist. In 1888 A.D. Van Gogh painted a pendant (a pair of works meant to be seen and compared together):

  • Van Gogh's Chair (1888, oil on canvas, The National Gallery, London) — a plain wooden rush-seat (straw-seat) chair in bright yellows and blues, with his pipe and tobacco on the seat; a daytime, open mood.
  • Gauguin's Chair (1888, oil on canvas, Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam) — a more ornate armchair in darker reds and greens, with books and a candle; a nighttime mood.

The two chairs stand in for two very different people. Van Gogh painted them while sharing a house with Paul Gauguin in Arles, France, the same year their friendship strained.

  • Copyright status: Public domain. Van Gogh died in 1890, well over 70 years ago (US life+70 rule), and both paintings were created and first exhibited in 1888. Safe to embed.
  • Images sourced:
  • Van Gogh's Chair was already embedded in this module as anchor-van-gogh-chair.jpg (pre-existing; not changed in this revision).
  • Gauguin's Chair is newly added in this revision. Downloaded from Wikimedia Commons (File:De_stoel_van_Gauguin_-_s0048V1962_-_Van_Gogh_Museum.jpg, tagged PD-Art / PD-old-100-expired, public domain), which is itself the Van Gogh Museum's own digitization (photographer Maurice Tromp, 2012) of the painting from its collection page https://www.vangoghmuseum.nl/en/collection/s0048V1962. Saved locally in this module folder as anchor-gauguin-chair.jpg (resized to 900px wide for web use; source Commons URL: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:De_stoel_van_Gauguin_-_s0048V1962_-_Van_Gogh_Museum.jpg), matching the local-file embedding convention already used for anchor-van-gogh-chair.jpg and established in Module 3.
  • Comparison added: the instructional page now shows both chairs in Part 1 (Look First) with a notice-and-wonder prompt when Gauguin's Chair is introduced, keeps the existing pendant comparison graphic in Part 2, and adds an explicit "Compare the pair" prompt to the Part 3 DAIJ walkthrough so students run Describe/Analyze on Gauguin's Chair as well as Van Gogh's Chair.
  • Sensitivity note: Van Gogh's mental-health struggles and his death are part of the historical record but are kept brief, factual, non-graphic, and age-appropriate in this cycle. Do not dwell on the ear incident or on his death in any student-facing material. If a student raises it, keep the response factual and brief.

Fact-check flags (verify exact wording/holdings before any formal report): - Van Gogh's Chair is held by The National Gallery, London. Gauguin's Chair (also titled Gauguin's Armchair) is held by the Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam. Confirmed against museum collection databases; both dated 1888. - Both are oil on canvas.

Discussion board (.03)

Template: 3. Art Critic's Corner. Twist (lead question): Van Gogh's Chair (1888) shows his own plain chair. He also painted Gauguin's Chair the same year. What can an empty chair tell us about the person who owns it? VR (.02)

Students choose a Location (an indoor space, a studio, or an outdoor scene), bring the two chair paintings from the instructional page into it, and look closely at texture, color, movement, and meaning. They answer three short questions (live with classmates or on their own), then draw one of the chairs or build a small chair-portrait scene of their own. Two sheets of plain white paper, a pencil, scissors, and color media (colored pencils, markers, or crayons). All standard household supplies; nothing to purchase.

Item Week Grading File

One teacher-graded event this cycle: the Week 2 monochromatic painting + statement, on a single 5-row rubric, one pass. Everything else is auto-graded or completion-scored. This holds the cycle to the 500:1 grading arithmetic.

Featured masterwork (verified)

Pablo Picasso (Spanish, 1881–1973). During his Blue Period (about 1901–1904 A.D.), Picasso painted almost entirely in shades of blue, producing melancholy, monochromatic works. A landmark example is The Old Guitarist (1903–1904 A.D., oil on panel, Art Institute of Chicago), an elderly musician rendered in many values of a single blue hue.

  • Keep all stated facts exact. The verified anchor facts are: Picasso's nationality and dates (Spanish, 1881–1973); the Blue Period span (about 1901–1904); the predominance of blue in that period; and The Old Guitarist (1903–1904, oil on panel, Art Institute of Chicago, acquired 1926 as the Helen Birch Bartlett gift, the first Picasso work to enter an American museum collection). Verify anything beyond this before adding it.

COPYRIGHT NOTE (read before any formal legal review of this course)

This module was flagged for a specific copyright rationale: that The Old Guitarist is safely public domain in the US because it was created and exhibited before 1928, and that "the Art Institute of Chicago, which holds it, publishes it as open-access/public domain." That second claim does not hold up under direct verification and should be corrected in any downstream summary:

  • The Art Institute of Chicago's own public API (api.artic.edu/api/v1/artworks/28067) returns "is_public_domain": false" for this specific object. It is not part of AIC's CC0 open-access image set, unlike many of the museum's other pre-1900 holdings.
  • The underlying legal rationale is still sound, however, and is independent of AIC's licensing choice: the painting was completed in 1903–1904 and has been on public display in the United States since at least 1926 (well before the 1928 cutoff for automatic US public-domain status), so it is public domain in the United States regardless of Picasso's 1973 death date and the life+70 rule that otherwise still protects his work.
  • Consistent with this, the image used here is not sourced from AIC. It is sourced from English Wikipedia's own (non-Commons) hosting of the file, File:Old_guitarist_chicago.jpg, tagged PD-US with the explicit rationale "first published outside the United States prior to January 1, 1931." The file lives on en.wikipedia.org rather than Wikimedia Commons precisely because the work is not yet public domain in Picasso's home countries (Spain/France use life+70, so it will not clear there until 2044), which is the same US-only safe harbor this module relies on. Local copy saved in this module folder as anchor-old-guitarist.jpg (downloaded from https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/b/bc/Old_guitarist_chicago.jpg, resized to 900px wide for web use).
  • Recommendation: treat this as safe to embed for US-based instructional use on the pre-1928 US-publication basis, but do not describe it in any formal/legal document as "AIC open-access" or blanket "public domain" without the US-only qualifier. The student-facing caption on the instructional page reads "Public domain in the United States (created and first exhibited before 1928)" rather than an unqualified "Public domain" for this reason.

Project-subject note (action item)

The course map lists this Quarter 3 project as "Vektor Painting." That title is almost certainly a typo or placeholder; it does not correspond to a known art technique or movement. This cycle builds the project as a clear Monochromatic Painting, which matches the module title, the Blue Period anchor, and the Elements/Principles focus. Confirm the intended project subject with the curriculum lead before final publication. If "Vektor" was meant to point to a specific named project, the studio brief in 05 can be retitled without changing its monochromatic structure.

Featured artist and movement (verified)

Michael Albert is a living American Pop artist known for what he calls "Cerealism": collages assembled from cut-up cereal boxes and other consumer product packaging. The featured work is his collage Froot Loops (created November 24, 1997), one of his best-known Cerealism pieces.

  • Collage (from the French coller, "to glue") is artwork made by gluing together pieces of paper or other materials.

Michael Albert is a living artist (born 1966), and his Cerealism collages remain under his copyright. His Froot Loops (1997) collage is not reproduced or embedded anywhere in this build — no image file was sourced, downloaded, or hotlinked for the deployed lesson.

Both are outside the scope of this curriculum build.

  • Michael Albert is an American Pop artist, living, born 1966, who calls his cut-and-collage cereal-box work "Cerealism."
  • Froot Loops is a Cerealism collage Albert made on November 24, 1997, built from a cut-up Froot Loops cereal box.
  • Over roughly three years Albert made more than 700 original Cerealism collages from cereal boxes and other packaging.
  • Albert also runs traveling, hands-on collage workshops for schools, libraries, and museums.
  • Collage (French coller, "to glue") is artwork made by gluing together pieces of paper or other materials.

Students choose a Location (a quiet indoor space, a studio, or an outdoor scene) and open Michael Albert's Froot Loops on his own website (link-out only, since the work is in copyright), alongside a real piece of packaging. Featured artwork (verified)

  • Both featured works are actively rights-managed (see COPYRIGHT NOTE below) and are not embedded on the instructional page. A clean link-out box on the page points to each authorized museum collection page instead:

COPYRIGHT NOTE

The review that generated this revision pass asked to "put in the actual artwork" of Campbell's Soup Cans (1962) and Marilyn Diptych (1962), describing them as public domain. That instruction is factually mistaken. Andy Warhol died in 1987. Both works are actively rights-managed by the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, and under the US life-plus-70 rule their copyright will not lapse until roughly 2057. Neither work qualifies for the pre-1928-publication exception that makes some other artists in this course (e.g., Picasso's The Old Guitarist, Module 13) safe to embed.

A digital file of Campbell's Soup Cans (Andy Warhol-CampbellsSoupCans-1962.jpg) exists in the course's provided source materials (01_Analysis\01_Analysis\Visual Art 3 Art Work\Pop Art Andy Warhol\). That file was not used in this build. Embedding it in a deployed, publicly reachable GitHub Pages lesson would be a real copyright violation, regardless of its presence in an internal working folder.

Instead, this build replaces both images with clean link-out boxes to the authorized holding museums, matching this course's existing pattern for in-copyright artists: - Campbell's Soup Cans — Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), New York: https://www.moma.org/collection/works/79809 - Marilyn Diptych — Tate, London: https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/warhol-marilyn-diptych-t03093

If the school wants the actual images embedded in the deployed lesson, that requires either (a) a paid license from the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts (or its licensing agent, the Artists Rights Society), or (b) a documented fair-use legal determination made by the school with counsel. Both are outside the scope of this curriculum build.

Featured masterwork (verified) — image embedded

Lorenzo Ghiberti (Italian, 1378–1455 A.D.), Gates of Paradise, the east doors of the Florence Baptistery (the Baptistery of San Giovanni, Florence), gilded bronze, executed 1425–1452 A.D. The doors hold ten square panels of Old Testament scenes built up in relief. Figures and architecture range from deep, nearly free-standing high relief in the foreground to very shallow low relief in the distance, so the bronze panels appear to recede into deep space even though they are only inches deep. The nickname Gates of Paradise is traditionally attributed to Michelangelo.

  • The original panels are conserved in the Museo dell'Opera del Duomo in Florence; a gilded replica hangs on the Baptistery today.
  • Image now embedded on 01_Week1_Instructional-Page.html, replacing the [IMAGE: ...] placeholder. Sourced from Wikimedia Commons: an 1855 albumen-print photograph of the whole doors, held by the Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (LCCN 2009631467). The photograph was published before 1931, so it is in the public domain in the US under the pre-1931 publication rule, independent of the underlying artwork's own public-domain status. Direct file: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a8/Lorenzo_Ghiberti%27s_%22Gates_of_Paradise%22_bronze_doors_depicting_scenes_from_the_Old_Testament%2C_Baptistry_of_St._John%2C_Florence_LCCN2009631467.jpg. The 1855 Library of Congress photograph was chosen specifically to avoid that complication and give a cleanly public-domain image.
  • Briefly named on the page as other examples of relief, all verified and standard: ancient Egyptian tomb and temple reliefs, Assyrian palace reliefs, and the Parthenon frieze (Athens, 5th century B.C.). No images required for these.

Discussion board (.03)

  • Grading (10 pts):
Criterion Pts

Uses at least 2 art vocabulary words correctly 2
2 replies that are respectful, specific, and add a new idea 4

  • VA.68.H.1.1: identify works as reflections of culture, time, and place. Verify current benchmark language at cpalms.org.

VR (.02)

Students choose a Location (a quiet indoor space, a studio, or an outdoor scene) and open Riley's Movement in Squares from the museum link on the Module 19 Instructional Page (link-out only, since Riley's work is in copyright). They put the photo of their own Module 19.01 sketch on a wall or board in their space, hunt for line, contrast, pattern, and the illusion of movement, answer three questions, and make an optical pattern of their own by drawing or building. Outside VR the same steps work from the museum page on screen and the sketch on paper, with Part 3 done on paper or with objects at a desk. Evidence is a screenshot or photo plus typed answers. The page opens with the line: if you can complete this in VR, do so; if not, it still needs to be completed outside VR.

Featured artist and works (verified)

Bridget Riley (British, born 1931) is a leading figure of Op Art (short for "optical art"). She became famous for precise black-and-white patterns that seem to move, ripple, or vibrate, and she later moved into color. Verified works referenced in this cycle:

  • Movement in Squares (1961) — a field of black-and-white squares that compress toward a vertical seam, so the flat surface appears to fold or dip. Held by the Arts Council Collection, Southbank Centre, London.
  • Blaze (1964) — concentric zigzag lines that seem to spin and flicker around a center. Held by Tate, London.

Victor Vasarely (Hungarian-French, 1906–1997) is often called a father of Op Art. This cycle also references one specific, verified Vasarely work:

  • Vega-Nor (1969) — oil on canvas, a flat grid of black, white, and gray shapes that appears to bulge outward like a sphere. Held by the Buffalo AKG Art Museum (Buffalo, NY; acquired 1969, accession K1969:29).

The 1965 exhibition The Responsive Eye. Op Art gained wide public attention through a landmark 1965 exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), New York, curated by William C. Seitz. The Responsive Eye was a large group show, not a single artwork by any one artist. It brought together roughly 125 works by many Op Art artists, introducing the style to a wide American audience for the first time; both Riley and Vasarely were among the artists featured.

COPYRIGHT NOTE (important — read before building or updating this module)

This module's original draft needed two corrections, both resolved in this revised build:

1. Living-artist / no-embed correction. Bridget Riley is a living artist (b. 1931), and Victor Vasarely died in 1997; his estate's copyright runs for his life plus 70 years, so his work will not enter the public domain in the US until roughly 2067. Neither artist is public domain. Even though real local image files for two Riley works (Movement in Squares and Blaze) exist in this course's 01_Analysis source-materials folder, they must not be embedded in Canvas, the instructional page, or anywhere else in this module. The instructional page instead uses clean link-out boxes pointing to authorized museum collection pages, verified live at build time: - Bridget Riley, Movement in Squares (1961), Arts Council Collection: https://artscouncilcollection.org.uk/artwork/movement-squares - Bridget Riley, Blaze (1964), Tate: https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/riley-blaze-p05083 - Victor Vasarely, Vega-Nor (1969), Buffalo AKG Art Museum: https://buffaloakg.org/artworks/k196929-vega-nor

Students study Op Art from these authorized sources and then create their OWN original optical pattern. The pure-CSS optical pattern demonstration built into the instructional page is original code, not a reproduction of any Riley or Vasarely work, so it may stay embedded.

2. Exhibition-vs-artwork correction. An earlier draft of this module's review notes referred to "Victor Vasarely's imagery associated with The Responsive Eye" as though The Responsive Eye were a Vasarely artwork or a body of his imagery. That is inaccurate. The Responsive Eye was the name of a 1965 Museum of Modern Art group exhibition, curated by William C. Seitz, that introduced Op Art to a wide American audience. It featured roughly 125 works by many artists, including both Bridget Riley and Victor Vasarely, but it is not a title that belongs to any single work by either of them. This revised build corrects the student-facing text to describe The Responsive Eye accurately as the historic exhibition, and separately features one specific, real, verified Vasarely artwork (Vega-Nor, 1969) with its own authorized link-out.

Teacher Cycle Plan — Module 20: End of Year Review — Portfolio Showcase & Art Show

M/J Visual Art 3 (CPALMS 0101120) · Grade 8 · Quarter 4 · 2-Week Cycle

Revision note (2026-10-14): Semester 2 format revision per "VA 3 Semester 2 REVISIONS.docx". Teacher-facing only. Benchmark codes and the answer key live here, never on student pages.

This is a review and showcase module, not a normal new-artwork cycle. Students do not make a brand-new project. They look back over the whole year, curate their strongest work, present it in a year-end art show, and reflect on their growth. This module realizes the Portrait-of-a-Graduate portfolio: the curated, reflected-upon body of work that demonstrates a student's artistic development across the year.

VR removal note (Module 20 specific)

The prior build's 03_Week1_VR-Session.html ("The Year-End Gallery Walk") is removed per the course-wide VR-removal directive, the same as every other module. This module's VR session was a three-part gallery-walk activity: (1) hang curated work on a VR wall, (2) walk classmates' galleries and note what to admire, (3) reflect on personal growth. Removing it does not require inventing a replacement Tier 1 file — the cycle's remaining components already carry the substance of parts 1 and 3:

  • Curation (VR Part 1's setup) is already the job of 02_Week1_Sketch-Assignment.html ("Curate Your Mini-Gallery"), which has students choose their 3–5 strongest works and explain why.
  • Personal reflection (VR Part 3) is already the job of the Week 2 Portfolio Showcase's four-to-six-sentence Year-End Reflection, which is more substantial than the VR exit reflection ever was.
  • Peer viewing (VR Part 2) is the one piece with no non-VR equivalent left in the cycle. It is not replaced with a new required, teacher-graded deliverable, since the course-wide rule holds the cycle to one graded event and Tier 1 items must stay low-friction. If a teacher wants to keep a peer-viewing moment, the simplest options are: (a) a live class session where students screen-share their OneDrive portfolios in turn, or (b) an ungraded Canvas discussion board thread where students post 1–2 portfolio images and reply with a genuine compliment to two classmates. Either is optional and teacher-run; it is not a required student component of this written cycle.

With the VR session removed, Week 1 is now: Instructional page (content) → Curate Your Mini-Gallery (Tier 1, completion) → Cumulative Final Review quiz (Tier 1, auto-graded). Week 2 is unchanged: the Portfolio Showcase + Year-End Reflection (Tier 3).

Which Element or Principle did you use most on purpose in it, and how does that choice show how you have grown since the start of the year? VR (.02)

This is now a solo walk through the student's own portfolio. The student chooses a Location (a quiet indoor space, a studio, or an outdoor scene), displays the three to five works chosen in .01 on a wall or board, labels them, walks through them in order as the curator, and answers two reflection questions. Outside VR the student lays the works out on a table or floor, or arranges the images on screen, and does the same steps on paper. Evidence is a screenshot or photo plus typed notes and answers. Peer viewing now happens in the .03 Discussion Board (Gallery Walk). The page opens with the line: if you can complete this in VR, do so; if not, it still needs to be completed outside VR.

Year-in-review content (verified, as taught)

This module reviews the whole year. The instructional page and the cumulative quiz draw only on facts as the course taught them. Key reference points (all verified against the module instructional pages):

  • Module 1 — Elements of Art: the seven Elements; Hokusai, The Great Wave off Kanagawa (c. 1831 A.D.).
  • Module 2 — Ancient Greece: the Parthenon (c. 447–432 B.C.); three column orders Doric, Ionic, Corinthian; value/form.
  • Module 3 — Ancient Rome: the Alexander Mosaic (c. 100 B.C., House of the Faun, Pompeii); tesserae; pattern and rhythm. (Vesuvius eruption A.D. 79.)
  • Module 4 — Day of the Dead: José Guadalupe Posada (1852–1913), La Calavera Catrina (c. 1910–1913); symmetry and balance.
  • Module 6 — Italian Renaissance: Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519 A.D.), The Last Supper (c. 1495–1498 A.D.); one-point perspective, horizon line, vanishing point, orthogonal lines.
  • Module 7 — Color Theory: primary/secondary colors, contrast, silhouette (J.M.W. Turner, The Fighting Temeraire featured).
  • Module 9 — Value: Rembrandt van Rijn (1606–1669) self-portrait; chiaroscuro; value scale. (Caravaggio's extreme version is tenebrism.)
  • Module 12 — Post-Impressionism: Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890), Van Gogh's Chair (1888 A.D.); expressive color, texture, movement.
  • Module 13 — Monochromatic: Pablo Picasso (1881–1973), The Old Guitarist (1903–1904 A.D., Blue Period); tint, shade, value.
  • Module 14 — Pop Art Cerealism: Michael Albert; collage; Pop Art.
  • Module 15 — Pop Art Warhol: Andy Warhol (1928–1987), Campbell's Soup Cans (1962 A.D.); repetition, pattern, rhythm, unity, positive/negative space; relief printing.
  • Other Q3/Q4 modules reviewed at the level of concept (analogous colors, watercolor, space art, Dragon's Eye, Grant Wood, digital art, clay relief, Op Art) without asserting new artist facts.

Sketch: Stars and Swirls
Assignment · 10 pts · Completion
📖 WHAT THIS PRACTICES
Three galaxy painting techniques
Wet-on-wet blending, a movement swirl, and a star splatter
This sketch is your practice rung. Before you paint your full Glimpsing Galaxies artwork next week, you will try each technique on its own, in a small space, with no pressure to make it perfect. Artists have always learned this way: study how something works, then try it yourself, one move at a time.
Lesson focus: Movement, Contrast, and Painting Techniques
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Divide one page into three boxes. In each box, practice one galaxy painting technique: a wet-on-wet color blend, a swirl that creates movement, and a splatter of white stars. This is a warm-up, so it is not meant to be perfect. Focus on learning how each technique behaves in your hand, not on making a finished picture. Plan to spend about 20 to 40 minutes.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What does each galaxy technique actually do when you try it with your own hand and brush?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Take one sheet of paper and divide it into three boxes. Label them: Box 1 "Wet-on-Wet Blend," Box 2 "Movement Swirl," Box 3 "Star Splatter."
2
Box 1: Wet-on-Wet Blend. Brush a little clean water or wet paint into the box, then drop in two or three cool colors (such as blue and violet) while it is still wet. Watch them melt together with no hard edge.
3
Box 2: Movement Swirl. Paint a sweeping spiral or swirl that curves around a center. Try to make your eye want to follow the curve. That pull is movement.
4
Box 3: Star Splatter. Paint the box a dark color first if you can. Once it is set, flick tiny white dots across it using an old toothbrush or by tapping a loaded brush. Notice how the bright dots pop against the dark: that is contrast. If you have no paint, use a white pencil or gel pen on a dark-shaded box.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All three boxes are labeled with the correct technique name.
☐
Each box clearly attempts its technique: a blend, a swirl, and a splatter.
☐
The page shows genuine effort and exploration, even if it is rough.
📊 HOW THIS IS GRADED
This is a completion grade. It is not judged on artistic skill. You earn full credit by submitting on time and showing real effort on all three boxes.
✓
Submitted on time
✓
Clearly addresses the task: all three boxes labeled and attempted
✓
Shows genuine effort and exploration
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

Photograph your page in good light with no shadows across it, and upload it as a JPG or PNG. (If paint is still wet, let it dry first so it photographs clearly.)

Activity · 10 pts · Completion
If you can complete this assignment in VR, please do so. If not, it still needs to be completed outside VR.
🥾 WHAT YOU WILL DO
Choose a Location for your space and bring in the deep-space images from the Module 11 Instructional Page. Display them on a wall or board in your space, or keep them on your screen or on paper if you are working outside VR. You will hunt for movement, contrast, color, and value in what you see, think through a few questions, and then make something of your own. Move through the three parts in order.
Location: your choice (a quiet indoor space, a studio, or an outdoor scene all work).
Vija Celmins is a living artist, so her galaxy print is not shown here. Open it on the museum's own page: Untitled (Galaxy) at SFMOMA.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
When you look at deep space, what creates the sense of motion and depth, and how could you put that on paper?
💡 BEFORE YOU BEGIN
Reopen the Module 11 Instructional Page and reread the two key ideas: movement, the flow that leads your eye, and contrast, the jump from dark to bright. Keep your vocabulary list nearby: movement, contrast, value, color. Have your notebook open so you can jot answers as you go.
📝 IN YOUR SPACE
Part 1 · Deep-Space Hunt · about 12 minutes
Look slowly at the deep-space images from the Instructional Page and the Celmins print, from the brightest cluster to the darkest stretch of sky. In your notebook, find and name where you see each idea at work:
▶  Movement: where do swirls or curves lead your eye on a path?
▶  Contrast: where is the strongest jump from dark space to bright light?
▶  Color: which colors glow through the dark, and how many can you count?
▶  Value: find the darkest spot and the lightest spot near each other.
Part 2 · Talk About It · about 10 minutes
Think through these three questions. They move from what you see, to what it means, to what you decide:
1. What creates the strongest sense of motion in the images, and why?
2. How does the contrast between dark and bright change how deep the space feels?
3. Does seeing the images displayed large, instead of small on a page, change the feeling? How?
IF YOU ARE IN A LIVE SESSION
Take turns. Share your answer to one question, then listen to a classmate and say whether you agree or disagree and why.
IF YOU ARE ON YOUR OWN
Write or record one or two sentences answering each of the three questions. Speak as if you were explaining the view to someone who had never seen it.
Part 3 · Make Something · about 10 to 15 minutes · choose one
Option A: Draw. Sketch your own swirling galaxy, using the drawing tools in your space or pencil and paper. Focus on just two ideas: a curving swirl that creates movement, and a clear jump in value from dark space to bright light. Note what gives it motion and depth.
Option B: Build. Build a small star-field or nebula scene, using objects in your space or objects at a desk (a dark cloth, foil scraps, cotton balls, a flashlight). Place bright points and a glowing cloud against the dark, with some near you and some far away. Note what creates the sense of motion and depth, and be ready to explain your choices.
✅ BEFORE YOU LEAVE
Write one sentence in your notebook: what will you most want to get right in your Module 11.04 Studio Project & Reflection, movement or contrast? What you noticed today will help you build it.

✓

Module 11.04
Studio Project & Reflection: Glimpsing Galaxies
Assignment · 100 pts
🎨 YOUR PROJECT
A painted galaxy, glimpsed through a broken wall
Built with movement, contrast, and the three techniques you practiced, finished with a cut-paper wall overlay
This is the one teacher-graded project of this module. You will paint your own galaxy or nebula, putting to work the same ideas you watched Vija Celmins use: strong contrast between dark and bright, and movement that leads the eye. Last week you practiced the techniques one at a time. Now you bring them together into a single deep-space painting, and then you finish the piece by breaking open a brick wall on a separate sheet and gluing it over your painting, so a viewer glimpses your galaxy through a hole broken in the wall, as if they had stumbled on a hidden view of deep space.
Lesson focus: Movement, Contrast, Color, and Value
📋 ELEMENTS AND PRINCIPLES FOCUS
Movement (a swirl or sweep that leads the eye), contrast (dark space against bright light), and the color and value choices that make space feel deep. You will build these with wet-on-wet blending, layering, and splatter, then complete the piece with a cut-paper brick-wall overlay that frames your glimpse of the galaxy.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Can you make flat paper feel like deep, moving space that someone could fall into, and glimpsed as if by accident?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Lay the dark background. Cover the whole paper with a dark, wet-on-wet background. Blend two or three colors that sit near each other, such as midnight blue, violet, and black, while the paint is still wet so they melt together with no hard edges. This deep dark is what will make your light glow later.
2
Build the galaxy with movement and contrast. Shape a galaxy or nebula that has a clear sense of movement: a spiral or a sweeping swirl that leads the eye. Keep a strong contrast between the dark space and the bright light at its heart.
3
Layer the glow. Once your base is dry enough, layer lighter colors (pale blue, pink, gold, or white) over the brightest area to build a soft glow. Add the light a little at a time, letting layers dry between coats.
4
Splatter the stars. When the painting is dry, flick tiny white dots across it with an old toothbrush or a tapped brush to scatter stars. Add a few larger dots for close, bright stars and many tiny ones for distant stars.
5
Break open a wall to reveal your galaxy. Once your painting is completely dry, take a separate sheet of paper for the overlay. Near the center of that sheet, draw a broken opening in the shape of an oval, rough and jagged at the edges rather than a neat, even ellipse, so it reads as a hole broken through something solid. Draw a brick wall pattern across the rest of the sheet, right up to the edges of that oval opening, so the page reads as a solid brick wall with one hole broken through it. Carefully cut out the oval opening and set the brick-wall piece aside. Glue the brick-wall piece on top of your painted galaxy, lining up the broken opening so your galaxy shows through it. The finished effect: a viewer glimpses your galaxy as if peering through a hole broken open in a brick wall.
6
Sign your work. Add your name to the front or back of the finished piece. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.
💡 HELPFUL TO KNOW
No special paint is needed. Watercolor, tempera, or acrylic all work, and even watered-down paint will do. If your paint dries too fast for wet-on-wet, lightly wet the paper with clean water first. The darker your background, the brighter your stars and glow will look: that is contrast doing its job. For the brick-wall overlay, a plain sheet of paper, a pencil, scissors, and glue or a glue stick are all you need; you do not need real bricks or clay. When you cut the oval opening, cut slowly and away from your hand; ask an adult for help with the tight curve if it feels tricky.
✅ WHAT MAKES A STRONG PIECE
☐
The galaxy or nebula has a clear sense of movement: a swirl or sweep that leads the eye.
☐
Strong contrast between dark space and bright light makes the light seem to glow.
☐
You used the techniques: a blended background, layered glow, and splattered stars; craftsmanship is neat.
☐
The brick-wall opening is cut cleanly and glued neatly, so the finished piece reads as a galaxy glimpsed through a broken wall, not two separate pieces stuck together.
☐
Your artist statement names a choice you made and something you discovered.
☐
The piece is complete and signed.
✍️ ARTIST STATEMENT
In the submission text box, write one or two sentences in your own voice about the piece you just made:
▶  How did you create movement or contrast in your galaxy, and why?
▶  What did you discover or find tricky while painting it, or while building the broken-wall overlay?

🎨 YOUR PROJECT
A repeated, color-varied relief print
Press one design into a foam plate, then print it again and again as a grid or mandala
This is the one teacher-graded project of this module. You will make your own printing plate from a clean foam tray, no cutting tools needed, and pull a print from it many times. Then you will arrange your repeats into a grid or a radial mandala, varying the color like Warhol did, paying close attention to positive and negative space and to unity across the repeats.
Lesson focus: Repetition, Pattern, Unity, and Positive/Negative Space
📋 WHAT YOU NEED
A clean, flat foam food tray or a foam sheet (the kind some produce or to-go food comes in, washed and dried), one dull pencil or a ballpoint pen, paint or ink, a small brush or a roller if you have one, several sheets of paper, and a center sheet to print your final design on. All standard household items. If you do not have a foam tray, the flat lid of a foam cup or any thin foam packaging works.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Can you repeat one pressed design so that the repeats, and the negative space between them, hold together as one unified work?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Draw your design. On scrap paper, draw one simple radial or mandala design that fits inside a square a little smaller than your foam tray. Keep the lines bold and simple. Remember: where you press is the negative space, and the flat raised foam left untouched is the positive space that will hold the ink.
2
Press the plate. Lay your drawing on the clean, flat part of the foam tray. Trace firmly over every line with a dull pencil or ballpoint pen, pressing a groove into the foam. Then lift the paper and press the lines directly into the foam a second time so the grooves are deep and clear. This foam tray is now your printing plate. No cutting tools are needed.
3
Ink the plate. Roll or brush a thin, even layer of paint or ink over the whole raised foam surface. The pressed grooves stay lower, so they pick up little ink. The raised areas carry the color. Work quickly so the paint does not dry before you print.
4
Pull the print. Press a sheet of paper onto the inked plate. Rub gently across the whole back with your hand, then peel the paper off to reveal your print. Pull a few practice prints first; relief printing gets better after the first try or two.
5
Repeat and arrange. Re-ink and print your design several more times. Arrange the repeats into a grid (like Warhol's soup cans) or rotate them around a center point into a radial mandala. Vary the color from print to print the way Warhol did, and keep the negative space between the repeats even so the whole work reads with unity.
6
Sign your work. When the print is dry, add your name in a corner. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.
💡 HELPFUL TO KNOW
A thin layer of paint gives a crisper print than a thick one. If your lines fill in with color, you pressed too lightly into the foam, so press the grooves deeper and try again. Letting each print dry a moment before placing the next keeps your colors from smearing into one another.

One design is printed several times and arranged as a clear grid or radial mandala.
☐
The color varies across the repeats, the way Warhol changed colors in his print series.
☐
The negative space between repeats is even, so the whole work reads with unity.
☐

☐
The print is complete and signed.

Studio Project & Reflection: Half-and-Half Portrait
Assignment · 100 pts
🎨 YOUR PROJECT
One portrait, split down the middle
One half realistic, one half cartoon, united into a single face
This is the one teacher-graded project of this module. Starting from a photo of a face, you will draw a portrait split down the middle: render one half realistically with value and shading, and the other half as a cartoon with clean line and flat color. Then you will unite the two halves into one believable portrait. Durer painted himself as real as he could in 1500. Now you will show that you can command both ends of the spectrum in a single face.
Lesson focus: Realism to Cartoon: Digital Portraits
📋 ART TOOLS IN FOCUS
All five: Value, Color, Line, Contrast, Unity. The realistic half leans on value and color; the cartoon half leans on line and contrast; unity is what holds the two halves together as one face.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Can you make a realistic half and a cartoon half feel like one united portrait, not two drawings glued together?
💡 ANY FREE TOOL WORKS
Use any free drawing tool you can open: a free drawing app, a free phone or tablet app, or free browser-based drawing software. Layers help here: put your photo on one layer and draw over it on layers above. No device that draws? Print or trace from a photo on paper, draw both halves, and photograph the result. No specific or paid app is required.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Choose your face. Use a clear, front-facing photo of yourself, or a photo of a face you have permission to use. Open it in your drawing tool, or place it under a tracing layer.
2
Split it down the middle. Draw a light line down the center of the face. One side will be the realistic half, the other the cartoon half. Keep both eyes, the nose, and the mouth lined up across the center so the halves match.
3
Render the realistic half. Draw this half as it truly looks. Use gradual value to shade the form, and blended color for the skin and hair. Soften your edges. Let the shading make the face feel round and solid.
4
Render the cartoon half. Draw the same features simplified: a clean, bold line for the outlines, flat fills of color, and exaggerated simple shapes. Push the contrast higher than on the realistic side.
5
Unite the halves. Give the whole portrait unity: line up the features across the center, and use a connecting color scheme so the same family of colors appears on both sides. The viewer should read it as one face, not two.
6
Export the file. Save or export your finished portrait as a JPG or PNG. If you worked on paper, photograph it in good light.
7
Sign your work. Add your name somewhere on the image itself. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.
💡 HELPFUL TO KNOW
The hardest part is the seam down the middle. To unite the halves, keep the eyes level, match the height of the eyebrows and mouth across the center, and repeat one or two colors on both sides. A shared background color also pulls the two halves together.
✅ WHAT MAKES A STRONG PORTRAIT
☐
One half is clearly realistic (gradual value, blended color) and the other half is clearly cartoon (clean line, flat color).
☐
The features line up across the center and a connecting color scheme unites the two halves into one face.
☐
The craftsmanship is careful: clean lines, neat color, an even split down the middle.
☐
Your artist statement names a choice you made and something you discovered.
☐
The portrait is finished, exported as a JPG or PNG, and signed.
💡 GOING FURTHER (OPTIONAL)
If you would like to push this further, use your digital tool to add a small background element, a symbol, a color choice, or a short word, that speaks to a community or global concern you care about (for example, environmental care, kindness, or accessibility). This is optional and will not affect your grade, but digital tools are exactly the kind of technology artists use to raise concerns bigger than themselves.

▶  What did you do to unite the realistic half and the cartoon half into one face?
▶  What did you discover or find tricky while making it?
For example: "I used the same warm browns on both halves and kept the eyes level so the face feels like one person, and I learned that the cartoon side needed a much bolder line than I expected to hold up next to the shaded side."

🎨 YOUR PROJECT
A clay relief built from your plan
Turn your flat design into real 3D form, using low relief and high relief
This is the one teacher-graded project of this module. You will press out a flat slab of clay and build your design up off it, raising some parts high and keeping others low, so the scene reads as three-dimensional form. Ghiberti turned a few inches of bronze into a whole world on the Gates of Paradise. Now you will turn a slab of clay into your own relief.
Lesson focus: From 2D shape to 3D form
📋 WHAT YOU NEED
Air-dry clay is the recommended material for this project. A brand such as Crayola Model Magic or a similar air-dry clay works well because it needs no kiln and no baking, just time to dry, so it is easy to use at home. If air-dry clay is not available, a simple no-bake salt dough mixed at home is a good substitute (see the tip below for how to mix it). Plus a flat board or surface, a butter knife or craft stick for carving, a pencil, and a few household items for texture: a fork, a bottle cap, a comb, leaves, lace, or buttons. Optional: paint and a brush for after the relief dries. Nothing special needs to be bought.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Can you raise and lower the clay so a flat slab reads as real, three-dimensional form?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Roll a slab. Press or roll your air-dry clay flat on a board until it is about a half inch thick. This flat slab is your background.
2
Draw your design. Using your Week 1 plan, lightly draw your design into the surface of the slab with a pencil or craft stick.
3
Build up and carve down. Build some parts UP by adding and smoothing on extra clay so they rise high off the slab (high relief). Carve other parts DOWN, or leave them low, so they stay close to the background (low relief). The difference in depth is what makes the scene read as 3D form.
4
Add texture. Press household tools into the clay to add texture: a fork for lines, a bottle cap for circles, lace or a leaf for patterns. Texture brings your relief to life.
5
Dry, then paint (optional). Let the relief dry fully. Air-dry clay and salt dough both need time, so start early in the week. Once it is dry, you may paint it if you like.
6
Sign your work. Carve or write your name on the back of the relief. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.
💡 HELPFUL TO KNOW
When you add clay on top of the slab, score (scratch) both surfaces first and press a little water between them so the new clay sticks and does not crack as it dries. To mix salt dough, combine about two parts flour, one part salt, and enough water to make a firm dough. When carving, always push the butter knife or craft stick away from your other hand, and work on a flat, stable surface so the clay does not slip.
✅ WHAT MAKES A STRONG RELIEF
☐
The relief uses both high relief and low relief, so the design clearly reads as 3D form, not a flat slab.
☐
The clay is handled with care: smooth joins, no cracks, neat edges.
☐
Texture is added with tools, and the design shows your own choices.
☐
Your artist statement names a choice you made and something you discovered.
☐
The relief is complete and signed on the back.

▶  Which part did you raise the highest, and why?
▶  What did you discover or find tricky while turning your flat plan into 3D form?

Line, Contrast, and the illusion of movement
This sketch is your practice rung. Before you design your full Optical Illusion artwork next week, you will try one Op Art trick by hand: warping evenly spaced lines around a hidden guide so a flat page seems to bulge. Artists have always learned this way: study how something works, then try it yourself.
Lesson focus: Line and the illusion of bulge
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
On one sheet of paper, draw a row of evenly spaced straight lines with a ruler. Then warp those lines around a hidden circle or wave so the flat page seems to bulge or dip. Where a line crosses your hidden guide, bend it: push the line so it curves around the circle or wave, then return to straight on the other side. Each line bends a little more as it gets closer to the center of the guide.
4
Go over your lines with a black marker or pen so the contrast is strong, then erase the pencil guide. Step back. The flat page should seem to bulge or dip where the lines bend.

🎨 YOUR PROJECT
Your own original Op Art illusion
Built from line, contrast, and pattern, so a flat page seems to move
This is your one teacher-graded project of the module. You will design and draw your own optical illusion: evenly spaced lines that bend around a guide and strong contrast that makes the flat page seem to bulge, dip, or vibrate. The sketch was your practice. Now you build the full illusion. This is your own original design, not a copy of any other artist's work.
Lesson focus: Line, contrast, and the illusion of movement
📋 OP ART FOCUS
Three tools do the work: Line (evenly spaced, then warped), Contrast (black and white, or two bold contrasting colors), and Pattern (a unit repeated and slightly changed). Together they create the illusion of movement on a flat surface.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Can you make a flat page seem to bulge, dip, or move using nothing but line, contrast, and pattern?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Draw a guide. Lightly sketch a guide shape in pencil: a grid, a circle, or a wavy contour. Press lightly. This guide is the hidden shape your lines will bend around.
2
Draw warped lines. With a ruler, draw evenly spaced lines across the page. Where they meet your guide, bend and warp them so the surface seems to bulge, dip, or move. Keep the spacing even so the illusion holds.
3
Add strong contrast. Fill alternating spaces so the page has bold contrast: black and white, or two bold contrasting colors. Strong contrast is what makes the illusion pop.
4
Keep it crisp. Make your lines clean and your spacing even. A blurry or uneven pattern breaks the illusion; a crisp, careful one makes the flat page seem to move.
5
Sign your work. Add your name to the artwork. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.
💡 HELPFUL TO KNOW
The illusion lives in the spacing. Where your lines bunch close together, the surface reads as far away or curving in; where they spread apart, it reads as bulging toward you. Plan your filled spaces before you commit to marker: once the contrast is down, it is hard to change.

☐
The flat page seems to bulge, dip, or move. The illusion actually works.
☐
Lines are evenly spaced and warped around a guide; the contrast is strong and bold.
☐

▶  What is one thing you genuinely admire about the piece?
IF YOU ARE ON YOUR OWN
Walk through your gallery on your own and write your notes. Speak your admiring comment aloud as if you were a visitor talking to the artist.
IF YOU ARE IN A LIVE SESSION
Take turns. Walk through your own gallery and share one Element or Principle you notice and one honest compliment about a piece, then listen to a classmate do the same.
Part 3 · Reflect and Respond · about 8 to 10 minutes
Stand back and look at your year displayed together. In your notebook, answer these two questions in a sentence or two each:
1. Looking at your works side by side, where do you see the clearest growth from the start of the year to now?
2. From this year of work, what is one idea or technique you would like to try again in your own future work?
✅ BEFORE YOU LEAVE
This activity is a completion grade. You earn full credit by taking part and capturing the simple evidence below.

✓

Module 20.04
Studio Project & Reflection: Portfolio Showcase + Year-End Reflection
Assignment · 100 pts
🎨 YOUR FINAL PROJECT
A curated portfolio of your best work from the whole year
Your strongest pieces gathered together, plus a reflective artist statement
This is the capstone of your year and the one teacher-graded project of this module. You will not make a brand-new artwork. Instead you will gather the curated works you chose last week into one polished portfolio, present them clearly, and write a reflection that looks back at how you grew as an artist. This is the project that pulls the whole year together.
Lesson focus: Portfolio Showcase + Year-End Reflection
📋 WHAT YOUR SHOWCASE INCLUDES
Two parts in one submission: (1) photos of your three to five curated works, presented neatly, and (2) a reflective artist statement of about four to six sentences that names specific Elements, Principles, and at least one artist or movement you learned this year.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
If a visitor saw only your portfolio, what would they learn about who you became as an artist this year?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Gather your curated works. Open your OneDrive portfolio folder and collect the three to five works you chose in your "Curate Your Mini-Gallery" assignment last week. If any photo is blurry or dark, re-photograph the original in good light if you still have it.
2
Label each work. For every piece, give it a short title or topic and name one Element or Principle it shows well (for example, "Roman mosaic: pattern and rhythm" or "Picasso study: monochromatic value").
3
Present it neatly. Make sure each photo is clear, well lit, and easy to read. Order your pieces so your portfolio flows, for example from your earliest work to your most recent so the growth shows.
4
Write your year-end reflection. In about four to six sentences, look back on your growth. Name specific Elements and Principles you got better at, and name at least one artist or movement you learned from. Use the prompt below to guide you.
5
Sign the showcase. Add your name and the words "Year-End Portfolio" so your collection is clearly yours. Every finished artist's portfolio carries its artist's name.
💡 HELPFUL TO KNOW
A strong reflection is specific. Instead of "I got better at art," try "I learned to use value and chiaroscuro to make a flat shape look round, the way Rembrandt did, and my Greek column study shows that." Naming the Element, the technique, and the artist makes your growth real and clear.
✍️ YEAR-END REFLECTION (ARTIST STATEMENT)
In the submission text box, write about four to six sentences in your own voice. Make sure your reflection does all of these:
▶  Names at least two specific Elements of Art or Principles of Design you got better at.
▶  Names at least one artist or movement you learned from this year.
▶  Tells what you are proudest of, and one thing that improved the most from the start of the year to now.
▶  Looks ahead: one thing you want to keep working on as an artist.
For example: "When the year began, value and space were just words to me. My favorite work is my one-point perspective drawing, because learning to use a vanishing point the way Leonardo da Vinci did in The Last Supper finally let me make a flat page look deep. I also improved most at value and chiaroscuro, which I used in my Rembrandt-style study to make a face look round. I am proudest of how my color mixing grew from the early color-theory module to my Van Gogh chair. Next, I want to keep working on texture and bolder brushwork."
✅ WHAT MAKES A STRONG SHOWCASE
☐
Three to five works are included, and they show real range across the year.
☐
The reflection names specific Elements, Principles, and at least one artist or movement.
☐
The reflection is thoughtful about your growth, not just a list of projects.
☐
Photos are clear, well lit, and presented neatly with labels.
☐
All parts are present and the showcase is signed.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1) Pts
Curation & Range
20 pts		 Three to five strong works chosen with clear care; shows real variety across the year. Good works chosen; some variety across the year. Few works, or all very similar; little range. One work or unclear selection. 20 pts
Reflection & Growth
20 pts		 Thoughtful, specific reflection on what improved and why; clear self-awareness. Clear reflection with some specific detail about growth. Vague or general; lists projects without reflecting. Minimal or missing reflection. 20 pts
Use of Art Vocabulary
20 pts		 Names Elements, Principles, and artists or movements correctly and naturally. Uses art vocabulary correctly, with a few terms. Few terms, or some used incorrectly. Little or no art vocabulary used. 20 pts
Presentation & Craftsmanship
20 pts		 Gallery is neat, clear, and well photographed; pieces are labeled and ordered with care. Mostly neat and clear; readable photos and labels. Uneven; some photos unclear or unlabeled. Hard to read; little care in presentation. 20 pts
Completion & Signature
20 pts		 All parts present: works, labels, reflection, and signature. Mostly complete and signed. Partially complete. Incomplete and/or unsigned. 20 pts
Total: 100 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Module 20.04 Studio Project & Reflection: Portfolio Showcase + Year-End Reflection
Upload the photos of your three to five curated works as JPG or PNG files, all in this one submission.
Type your year-end reflection directly into the submission text box, in the same submission as your photos.
Due: End of Week 2
Keep your full portfolio folder in OneDrive. It is the record of your whole year and a portfolio you can keep building on.
Last step: sign the showcase. Add your name so this year of work is unmistakably yours.
